utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor Markovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The cross-examination will now continue. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor. Yesterday, we finished talking about letters between you and Fehmi Agani. Next, I want to talk to you about Exhibit P456, and I think that's at tab 18 of your binder. And this comes from your testimony at page 13163 on the 8th of August. And in your testimony you mentioned -- or you took note of the -- part of the resolution that speaks about the commitment of all the member states to the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. But in that document there's also a call for international involvement in the negotiations and talks. I think that's item number 3 at the bottom of page 2. Do you recall that, Professor, that that was something that was being called for in that document?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that was something that the leaders of the bigger political parties on behalf of the Kosovar Albanians had been insisting on for some time, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they had been insisting on an international presence during the talks on representatives of the international community being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to move on to another topic. At page 13164 I think you were shown Exhibit P907, that's tab 19, and this was a decision by the National Assembly on a temporary or provisional Executive Council for the province of Kosovo. In English, we use the acronym T-E-C or TEC, I think in B/C/S it's represented by the initials P-I-V. Were you aware when that body was created in, I think, September of 1998?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In reviewing the documentation concerning that body, Professor, I see no prior discussion about the creation of such a body. Were you aware of any discussion in the National Assembly or in the political circles about creating the TEC or the provisional temporary Executive Council for Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was some discussion about setting up that body. There was a statement signed by President Milutinovic and Mr. Rugova, and the last paragraph of that statement says that work will be done on setting up a joint government, a joint provisional Executive Council for Kosovo and Metohija. That is the very last paragraph of their joint statement which they both signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is this some kind of body that's provided for in the Constitution of Serbia, the 1990 constitution?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Constitution of Serbia provides for three different kinds of bodies for the autonomous provinces, the 1990 constitution. A provincial Assembly, the provincial Executive Council, and the provincial organs of administration. What we're looking at here is a provisional Executive Council, if you like, because it wasn't elected by the Assembly of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija, which had itself not been constituted; rather, it was elected by the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And where is -- where in the constitution is the provision for a provincial Executive Council? Do you recall for what article that is?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll get to it, just a minute. I think it's in the grey binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm looking at Article 108 to 112 seem to talk about the autonomous provinces.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's Article 111, paragraph 1 says: "Organs of the autonomous province shall be: The Assembly, the Executive Council, and organs of administration." And paragraph 2 which reads: "The Assembly of an autonomous province shall comprise delegates appointed at direct elections by a secret vote," so that is the article envisaging the possibility of such a body.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how is that body selected? Is the Executive Council selected by the provincial Assembly?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The Executive Council is selected by the provincial Assembly. However, for the reasons already stated, because the elections had been boycotted by the Albanians and the Albanians had the majority population of Kosovo and Metohija, no autonomy was constituted in keeping with the constitution, such as had previously been the case in Vojvodina, for example. So the Executive Council was nominated, or rather, appointed, the chairman of the Executive Council by the National Assembly. Nevertheless, this is only a provisional transitional body, if you like, set up to deal first and foremost with humanitarian issues, with everyday issues arising in that area at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, the first point is I think you said this before, you said the provincial Assembly had not been re-instituted because the elections had been boycotted by the Albanians. Had any elections been scheduled for selection of a new Assembly in Kosovo after 1990?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need for that. They had by then boycotted the elections to the republican Assembly, the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia, thereby making it known that they had no wish to be involved in the establishment of any body or organ of the Republic of Serbia which they do not acknowledge as their own state. Secondly, they had set up parallel, the parallel system of government, parallel authorities, thereby making it known that they wanted to secede from the Republic of Serbia and that their intention and objective was to establish Kosovo and Metohija as an independent and sovereign state. They held elections for their own body's organs which they set up themselves and which were not set up in compliance with the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia. So this was the Assembly and the Government of Kosovo and Metohija. This was based on a constitution which the Albanians had adopted outside of the already-existing constitution and outside of the already-existing legal order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Professor, I understand your position about that but I think, given the way you've answered questions previously and insisted on being precise and legal and technically correct, it is not fair of you to say that the Kosovo Albanians boycotted elections for a provincial Assembly when no such elections were ever scheduled. Wouldn't you agree with me? You can't boycott something that doesn't exist.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't saying anything about boycotting the elections to the provincial Assembly, but to the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia. Those were the elections that were boycotted at the time. This was in December 1990, just after the constitution had been adopted. It was announced in no uncertain terms, given the fact the Albanians had already adopted the so-called Kacanik Constitution that they wanted to set up a system consistent with their own constitution and independent of the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia. They failed to -- they had previously failed to respond to get involved in the parliamentary elections to the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So you're saying now that they did not boycott elections for a provincial Assembly because no such elections were ever scheduled, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The elections had not been scheduled because no statutory decision preceded it which was to be adopted based on the constitutional law for the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia to be implemented. All this happened because at the time, back in 1990, the Albanians had adopted their own constitution and their intention was quite clear. It was based on that constitution that they had elections to their own bodies that they were establishing, including the election of their president. It was crystal clear that they had no desire whatsoever to join the constitutional system, the constitutional order, prevailing in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. And in the constitution under -- Article 73 is the provision that sets forth the powers for the National Assembly, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And there are 13 separate items listed under Article 73. Can you point to me in those 13 articles where they would have a power to create an Executive Council for the autonomous province?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no such power provided for by the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia, but there is such a power in the constitutional law on the implementation of the constitution. The wording should be here somewhere. I know that I have it in my bag. I'm not sure about its precise location in the binder, but if you want me to go back to that document I can quote it for you. The constitutional law on the implementation of the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance here, I think the last three pages of the same tab, number 5, is in fact the Law on Implementation of the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia. It is the part of the same exhibit, P855.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. I found it. It's Article 13, which says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would like it known that they don't have the original text in front of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The Assembly of the Republic of Serbia will adopt a provisional statutory decision for the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija and will schedule direct and secret elections to the provincial Assembly in compliance with the provisions of the constitution and the provisional statutory decision. The newly-elected Assembly of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija will have the status of a province" . Based on this, you can see that the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia is substituting provincial organs until such time as they are properly elected. This is the constitutional law on the implementation of the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, did you have a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There was a statement there by the interpreters that they didn't have the text, but I see we now have it. In my tab 5, there is no such document. It ends with Article 136.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You're right, Your Honours. We used the P exhibit, which is P855, and the Serbian version contains the Law on Implementation and right now I just saw that the translation does not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is a translation. It's now appeared on the -- oh, no, that's Article 13 of the Constitution, sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, that's Article 13 of the Law on the Implementation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I understand but what's appeared on the screen is the Article 13 of the Constitution. Are you saying that Article 13 of the Law on the Constitution has not been translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is my understanding, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that part of it will have to be, that particular article, and that should be done as a matter of priority.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We will give the instructions right now or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In fact, it may be unnecessary. Is that the only Article that is likely to arise here?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would say so. I mean it depends on what Mr. Hannis has to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness has already quoted it word for word so there's no need to go beyond that. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My binder is the same as yours, it ends with the last Article in the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, let me understand, though, when we were talking about the powers of the president before you explained to us that those powers enumerated in the constitution were all the powers that he had and that they couldn't be expanded by legislation. Now, it sounds to me like you're saying, although Article 73 lists the powers of the Assembly, this law on the implementation of the constitution appears to give them some additional constitutional powers. Is -- am I understanding correctly?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the constitutional law on the implementation of the constitution. It appears a transitional regime, a transition from the old constitutional order of the Republic of Serbia to the new Constitution of the Republic of Serbia. So we're looking at a transitional period. We're looking at a country that is organising itself along the lines of the 1990 constitution. Therefore, there is a transitional regime in place for a limited duration. It is only throughout this time that the Assembly has this particular power, the National Assembly. As for the president of the republic, the constitutional law on the implementation of the constitution gives him no exclusive powers whatsoever, not even for the short duration of this transition.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So then during this transitional period before the new constitution takes effect, does this constitutional law, in effect, act as the equivalent of a constitution? Is it an interim constitution?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The constitution took effect at the time it was adopted, the moment it was adopted. As soon as a constitution is promulgated, it takes effect. This is also enshrined in a provision of the constitution, both the 1990 constitution -- including the 1990 constitution, and this is what it says.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would like to know that we don't have the reference for the exact article of the constitution so we may quote it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is a constitutional law? And this is something we discussed on day one. It's a provisional act which only applies during a limited duration of time --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Professor, to interrupt. I see Mr. Zecevic is standing?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I see that the interpreters are asking for the reference to the article, it's Article 134 of the Constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, I'm sorry I interrupted you. Did you want to continue?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Article 134 and it tells you about what the constitutional law really is. If you look at the substance of the constitutional law there Article 1 -- paragraph 1 it says: "The constitutional law shall be enacted on the date as promulgated by the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia. If -- unless the constitution and this law say otherwise in terms of the implementation of its provisions," this is Article 1 of the constitutional law.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would like to know that we didn't have the text or the reference. The witness continues --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We understand that, this is a message to the interpreters, that you don't have it because it hasn't been translated. The Serb version is there if it helps, but I doubt if that is what you are looking for. So please try to bear with us while we deal with this. Please continue, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite simply, deadlines are defined here by which the bodies envisaged by the constitution shall be established as well as deadlines by which the laws mentioned in the constitutional law must be harmonized with the constitution. This is not a provisional constitution. This is an act which is meant to help implement the 1990 constitution. It ceases to apply as soon as one acts in compliance with it, as soon as the organs are set up envisaged in the constitution and organs envisaged in the constitutional law, once all of its provisions have been implemented and once all of its provisions have materialised. This is the purpose of the constitutional law. It is not meant to be any sort of a provisional constitution. There is the permanent constitution, in this case the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia from 1990, and the constitutional law merely makes it happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, Professor. You'll have to bear with me for a little bit because I'm having some difficulty. Article 134 is the one you were just reading from, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was reading from the constitutional law, the constitutional law on the implementation of the constitution. Article 134 is a constitutional article, and what I was reading was Article 1 of the constitutional law on the implementation of the constitution of the Republic of Serbia. As for Article 134 of the Constitution, it tells us what the constitutional law on the implementation of the constitution is, who adopts it, and how.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. But Article 134 is from the 1990 constitution, which took effect when?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It took effect the day it was promulgated by what then used to be the Assembly, the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Serbia. It's in Article 1 of the constitutional law. There are differences in terms of when a law takes effect and when a constitution takes effect. A law takes effect as soon as it is promulgated and a constitution takes effect as soon as it has been promulgated by the relevant body.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what date was that, that the constitution was promulgated by the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 28th of September, 1990. Under the text of the constitution there is the decision on the promulgation of the constitutional law on the implementation of the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia signed by the then-President of the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Zoran Sokolovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Then what was the effective date of the law on the implementation of the constitution, the constitutional law on the implementation of the constitution, what was its effective date?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says in Article 134, paragraph 4 of the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia, it says: "The constitutional law shall come into force simultaneously with the amendments to the constitution." Thus, it went into effect on the 28th of September, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the date that the National Assembly created the provisional Executive Council?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was done on the 28th of September, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, Article 134 is in a section of the constitution headed: "Amending the Constitution." And that plus the words used in Article 134 would suggest that the constitutional law to which Article 134 is referring is a law relating to the implementation of amendments to the constitution. Mr. Hannis's questions seem to be directed to the constitutional law by which the new constitution was implemented. Now, are you saying that's the same provision in spite of its words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The constitutional law for the implementation of the amendment to the constitution, regardless of the type of change, whether it was a new constitution or changing the constitution that was in effect, I didn't quite understand where the problem is, what the question exactly is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the section you're looking at which starts with Article 132, appears to relate to amending this new constitution; in other words, things that will happen in the future. Now, what we're concerned about is the implementation of this constitution in the first place, and Article 134 does not appear to me to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It pertains to the constitutional law for its own. How can I put it? The constitutional law that would be adopted in order to implement amendments to the constitution of 1990. The constitutional law that deals with changes or amendments to the constitution of 1974 also existed, and that is a document containing a provision in the constitution of 1974, and that constitution provides that amendments to that constitution -- before amendments can be carried out, a law on the implementation of the constitution needs to be adopted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So are you saying that the provision that Mr. Hannis is looking for is to be found in the 1974 constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. The constitution of 1974 in its last articles regulating the constitutional amendments, I think that constitution also is in the binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zecevic, your client seemed to be indicating that he could offer some assistance. You should be aware of that in case you want to take any instructions from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he's just commenting on the translation problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The language problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You mean part of the interpretation this morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, not the part of the interpretation, but the way what Professor is saying and how you understand that. And if I can be of assistance, tab number 9 is P1623, it's a Constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia of 1974, and it contains at the very end the Law on Amendments of the constitution -- but it's a federal, but I would assume that Professor can provide an explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This pertains to the federal constitution, but mutatis mutandis it applies also to the constitution of the federal units, the Republic of Serbia. And this is what the constitution says. It's Article 405 of the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia of 1974.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, do we not have the 1974 constitution for the Socialist Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid not, Your Honours. We were relying only on two particular articles of it, and that is what is in these binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We can provide also the document if needed, it exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hannis, do you wish to continue with this now?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I could hear the Professor read what Article 405 is, I could make a decision from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Could you read Article 405 please, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 405 of the Constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia of 1974, paragraph 1: "A special constitutional law shall be passed for the implementation of the present constitution and to ensure transition to its application." Paragraph 2: "The constitutional law pertaining to the implementation of the SFRY constitution shall be passed on the proposal of the Chamber of Nationalities by all chambers of the Federal Assembly. The draft of the constitutional law shall be adopted by a two-thirds majority vote in each chamber according to the provisions of paragraph 5, sections 4 to 8 of the constitutional amendment 12." Paragraph 3: "The draft constitutional law pertaining to the implementation of the SFRY constitution shall be promulgated and shall come into force simultaneously with the SFRY constitution."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have been able to find it, it's tab 74, P1848; however, in the binder we have just prepared the copies of the articles that we -- that we intended to rely on. But I'm sure in the e-court we have the whole translation. It's the Constitution of the Socialist Republic of Serbia of 1974, tab 74, P1848.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The tab appears to have a wide range of provisions translated, but these are a selection, are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, that is a selection, yes, Your Honours, because if we have added the whole translation it would have been tremendously big material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it doesn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's what we wanted to avoid, and it contains -- at the very end it contains the Law on Amendments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed we now have the correct document that the witness should be referring to. He's been dealing with provisions relating to the federal constitution --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you go to tab 74, Mr. Hannis, and you go to the end you'll get the provisions relating to the Constitution of the Socialist Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Professor, here is I think the heart of my confusion. If the new constitution, the 1990 Constitution for the Republic of Serbia, came into effect on the 28th of September, 1990, the National Assembly passed their decision on forming the provisional Executive Council for Kosovo on that same day. Now, I don't know, does it make a difference if the constitution was promulgated at 9.00 in the morning and the laws at noon or vice versa? But it seems to me if it happened on the 28th, then the constitution is in effect and the powers the National Assembly has are those set forth in Article 77, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 77?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Article 73, I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if you are asking if the constitution and the constitutional law were promulgated on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may be of assistance. I don't want to really get into the question, I just want to be of assistance. I assume my learned friend from the other side is talking about the establishment of the temporary Executive Council on the 28th of September but that happened eight years after, it is 28th of September, 1998, and the constitution was brought up on the 28th of September, 1990. So just to avoid -- if I was of any assistance. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And my question is: What provision in the constitution allowed for the National Assembly to create a provincial Executive Council? I don't see it in Article 73.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attempted to explain that on the basis of Article 13 of the constitutional law on the implementation of the constitution; this is a provision under that article. Since a statutory decision was not adopted and Kosovo and Metohija issues were ripe for resolution, there was no state body that could deal only with those issues, and specifically, in order to resolve those burning questions on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, I told you that this was also the subject of a joint statement of Mr. Milutinovic and Mr. Rugova. This organ was formed. It was a temporary organ. It's not an organ recognised by the constitution. The constitution recognises the Executive Council of the province, which was the Assembly of the autonomous province. Therefore, that is the nature of that body. It is of a temporary or transitional nature, in order to resolve burning questions in the lives of the population in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So in your expert opinion, Professor, is it constitutional, that act by the National Assembly?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the constitution and the constitutional law are looked at as a whole, then it was the constitution. But if you only look at Article 73 and not at the constitutional law for the implementation of the constitution, then it's not constitutional because Article 73 does not provide that the National Assembly should elect organs of the autonomous province. The autonomy of the autonomous province specifically consists of the voters of the autonomous province independently electing their representatives and their bodies. The state is not supposed to elect bodies and state organs in their stead. This was just an extraordinary situation in which the Republic of Serbia found itself, and that's why the organ is called a provisional Executive Council. It was necessary to have a body that would be of some use to the population of Kosovo and Metohija, and that was better than having no organ at all. This organ would not usurp any powers, it could not do anything bad. It could only act in the interests of the local population, the provincial population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That sounds, Professor, a bit like a pragmatic solution in a situation where there was no statutory provision to deal with that. Is that what you're describing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am referring the whole time to the constitutional law on the implementation of the constitution, Article 13, but I am explaining why the National Assembly elected a provisional Executive Council for Kosovo and Metohija without previously adopting a transitional statutory decision, as required by Article 13 of the constitution. But in view of what was happening on the ground, life and the actual situation, I am explaining the decisions by the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, I'll move on to another subject. Let's have a look at Exhibit 1D204, and I think this is in tab 27 of your red binder, Professor. This is Yugoslavia's endorsement of the Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement, and if we could look at page 3 of that document. At page 13169 Mr. Zecevic was talking to you about this and asked whether to the best of your knowledge did the government implement this agreement, or rather, these 11 points which it adopted in October 1998. And when he explained by "implement" he meant "carry out," then you said: "Yes." Do you have the document, Professor? I'm not going to talk about all 11 items, but I understood your answer to be: Yes, that Serbia did implement those or did carry those out. Could you look first at number 6 the legal arrangements establishing Kosovo and Metohija's self-governance and the legal frameworks of the Republic of Serbia and the Federal Republic Yugoslavia are to be harmonized in accordance with international standards in the Helsinki Final Act. First of all, can you tell me what the international standards are regarding self-governance of Kosovo. What did you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand if you mean the acts on the possible amendments to the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia and the Republic of Yugoslavia or if you are thinking of the act on self-governance in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I guess I'm trying to read the provision as a whole and understand what "international standards" means in the context in that document. Is that international standards for the self-governance of a province; and if I'm correct about that, what actions had Serbia taken to accomplish that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are international standards for the protection of minority rights. There are no international standards for territorial autonomy because this is an internal question and the -- and a question of the constitutional order of each individual country. The protection of minorities is a trans-national issue. There are international acts on the protection of minority rights, and here this is what that means, the protection of minorities. In acts of the Republic of Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia should be harmonized with international standards and the closing acts from Helsinki. I don't think it's here but I think this is 1999, I believe. It's not stated or it could be 1998. If we're talking about the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement, I think that a federal law was adopted on minority rights, which has a very exhaustive catalogue of minority rights which was later expanded and adopted by the Charter on Human and Minority Rights and Civic Freedoms adopted by the then-Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or the state union of Serbia and Montenegro in 2003. The Federation law I think was adopted in late 1998 or in 1999. I'm not exactly sure when.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you about number 7. It says: "Citizens in Kosovo and Metohija shall govern themselves democratically through Assemblies and executive and judicial organs of Kosovo and Metohija. Within nine months there will be free and fair elections for Kosovo, including those at the communal level." Now, it's noted here that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia invites OSCE to supervise those elections, but no such elections were ever held, were they, Professor? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about number 10: "No person will be prosecuted in state courts for crimes related to the conflict in Kosovo except for crimes against humanity and international law." That didn't happen, did it? Numerous people were prosecuted in the state courts for crimes related to the conflict in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know, because I'm not a judge. And as for the previous matter, that was not implemented because the Kosovo Albanians did not come --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't ask you that question. I just asked you for a yes or no to that previous question. Mr. Zecevic can follow-up if he would like. You say you weren't a judge -- you were a judge of the Constitutional Court at one time, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was a judge at -- in the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia. That's what it was called, the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia. That was its correct name according to the constitution of 1974.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you were one of the five deputy prime ministers for Serbia, and I understood you to tell us before that your portfolio was for law and legal matters, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for legislative -- judicial matters and the legal system. This was specified in the act of the president -- of the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So of the five deputy prime ministers, if it wasn't you who would be the one most likely to deal with matters regarding prosecutions and state courts, who would it be?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Questions of criminal prosecution is not something that executive organs deal with the government and its ministers but it's a matter for the courts. That is the sense of the constitutional principle on the independence of the judiciary. The government and the ministers have nothing to do with that aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Who deals with appointing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have to say, I find that difficult. We're talking here about a political agreement. Surely in the context of the political agreement you don't leave it to the prosecuting authorities to decide what to do. Surely you have an obligation to implement what has been undertaken, and that someone in the government must carry responsibility for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sorry, besides, things are of common knowledge as well. I mean a person who is a deputy prime minister would have a general knowledge of things.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that according to the government -- the Law on Government, the deputy prime minister has no duties established by law. He receives his duties from the prime minister. He doesn't have his portfolio. He receives his duties from the prime minister; but even if he was entrusted with a duty, he cannot exceed the bounds of the constitution. The constitutional principle is that the courts are independent in their work based and the constitution and the laws. The government cannot interfere in the work of the courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, then lastly would you look at Article 11: "The competent organs shall re-examine with the aim of extraordinary mitigation of the punishments, the sentences of the sentenced members of the national communities in Kosovo and Metohija for criminal offences motivated by political aims." Now, you said the other day that the -- all these were implemented or carried out. Was number 11 carried out; and if so, can you tell us when and how and by whom?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could not have said that all 11 provisions have been carried out because there was very little time available for that. This agreement was concluded in mid-October, and the negotiations in Rambouillet started in February; however, an effort was made to carry out what was attainable from this agreement, these 11 provisions. However, this last question also is within the realm of the judiciary and the government cannot interfere with the judiciary. I think that that's the way it is in your country, too, isn't it? That's the way it is in all orders based on checks and balances, and if you look at Article 9, the government is the executive. How can it intervene in judiciary matters? It doesn't have any competencies in terms of appointing or recalling judges, let alone having something to do with the judicial process as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, I would say that in my country probably judges and government officials would both say that the other interferes with their own business, but let me ask you about page 13171 of your testimony on the 8th of August. You mentioned that -- you mentioned the signing of the so-called Pristina Declaration. What document does that refer to? What was -- what was the item that you called the Pristina Declaration?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a document that was signed by those who took part in creating the agreement on self-governance in Kosovo and Metohija. That is to say, the delegation of the Government of the Republic of Serbia, the representatives of those two political parties of the Kosmet Albanians, and the representatives of all the ethnic communities that had taken part in formulating the provisions of that agreement. That is to say that the signing of that document, which on behalf of the federal government was signed by Mr. Vladan Kutlesic, well that's the declaration. That is the content of this Pristina Declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I thought that was the one you were referring to. And in conjunction with your testimony about that you mentioned Mr. Milutinovic came to Kosovo on that occasion, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in answering Mr. Zecevic's question about what in your view was the reason for that, you said that: "The high state official, the head of state, directly elected by the citizens, even though he had no strong effective constitutional power, wished by his presence to indicate the significance attached to those talks." But, Professor, if there was a real -- I suggest to you, if there was a real interest in showing how important Serbia thought these talks were, wouldn't it have been better to send someone who had effective operational control or power, perhaps somebody like the prime minister or the head of the National Assembly or even Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the government had chosen its delegation. In that way, the government ensured its presence, in all fairness not through the presence of the prime minister but through a delegation that they had chosen by themselves. Then the president is primus inter pares, he is a first among equals, the president of the Assembly that is, he is the Speaker of the National Assembly, he doesn't have any special rights of his own. It certainly could not have been President Milosevic, that possibility is ruled out because he was the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at that time. So it was only natural that the person who embodies the state of the Republic of Serbia, because all of it was happening in the state of the Republic of Serbia, should be present at that point in time, which was very important for the state entity and for resolving a burning issue in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in discussing that event Mr. Zecevic asked you about whether President Milutinovic had sent letters to the Albanian political leaders in connection with that, and you said that you remember that he had. He sent letters to both. He sent letters to the political leaders, the political leaders of the Albanian ethnic community, Mr. Qosja, Q-a-u-s-h-a is how it's spelled in the transcript, Mr. Hyseni and Mr. Demaqi. I want to show you an exhibit, this is Exhibit 1D062 [Realtime transcript read in error "1D tab 62"] -- and I don't have a tab number for this. I don't know if this was in the binder or not, but I do have a hard copy I can have the usher hand you and this should be in e-court. Professor, this is a series of individual letters. The first sheet appears to be a cover sheet of some sort from the archives, and you'll see in the upper left, I'm reading from my English, please tell me if I read something that's not consistent with the original B/C/S. But in the upper left it says: "Sent by President M. Milutinovic," there's a dated of 14 November 1998, this is a letter to I. Rugova and letter to members of the negotiating team, invitation to a meeting and discussions between the state delegation and the delegation of the DSK, Democratic League of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In case it's missed, Mr. Hannis, the quotation -- or the Exhibit is 1D62, is that correct --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have 1D062.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not tab 62. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no tab number for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then, Professor, the next page you should see the letter to -- or Dr. -- or Mr. Rugova it's entitled in the upper right it's dated Belgrade, the 14th of November, 1998 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I would avow to the Court and my learned colleagues that in 1998 the 14th of November was a Saturday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it's inviting him to a meeting. You'll see the next-to-the-last paragraph: "The meeting will be held in Pristina at 1100 hours on Wednesday, 16 November, 1998," and I inform you that the 14th of November the day the letter was sent was a Saturday, the 16th of November would have been a Monday and this says "Wednesday." Now, for one thing it's only two-days' notice and the other is, it's not clear whether it is on Wednesday, the 18th or whether it's on the 16th, which is a Monday. And you can see how the recipient of the letter might have had some confusion when the meeting was to take place, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have the calendar for 1998 in front of me. If you checked all of that out, then you're right. I take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I appreciate that. The next letters are identical letters to six other individuals, I think, and you'll see that they're all dated the 14th of November, 1998, and each of these I will tell you the next-to-the-last paragraph for each of these six is the same and it says: "The meeting will be held in Pristina at 1100 hours, on Wednesday, the 11th of November, 1998," three days before the letter was sent. And you can hardly blame the recipients of these letters for not making the scheduled meeting if the letter wasn't sent until three days after, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The addressee is Mr. Ljuan Koka who is the representative of the Roma ethnic community. He regularly responded to all invitations. I think that he attended all the meetings held, and this is exactly what is written here in the text that you gave to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go next to a related item, and this is Exhibit 1D623, tab 34 of your binder, Professor. And these are Mr. Milutinovic's closing remarks on the 18th of November, 1998, and I think this is in conjunction with that Pristina agreement that you told us about. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm reading from paragraph 2 in the English, and tell me if I say anything that's not consistent with your Serbian version. "Unfortunately, our meeting today was not attended by the representatives of leading political parties of Albanians from Kosmet. This is not the first time that they did not respond to our calls to a political dialogue. Such an attitude of these political parties in itself speaks a lot to our public and all those well-intentioned in the world because any further delay and refusal under lame and transparent excuses and conditionalities can only result in derailing the process of searching political solutions." And further on there are a couple of remarks regarding this failure to attend the meeting. Professor, with regard to Dr. Rugova it seems that there was some confusion about the letter that went out to him scheduling the meeting and to me it seems unfair to have blamed him for failing to attend, given the nature of that invitation. And I wonder if you have a comment about that.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about tab 34, I do not have the text that you just read out in front of me. I did follow it, but I could not check how good the translation was, how faithful it was, the English translation. I talked about the letters that I had signed as head of the delegation for the talks. Now, in the letters that you gave me there is this obvious discrepancy in the dates, and that can certainly create confusion. Because how can one behave if one receives a letter on the 14th of November and it has to do with a meeting scheduled on the 11th of November; that is to say that the meeting was already over by the time you received the letter of invitation. Although I find this hard to explain. This is the first time I see this. The only way I can interpret this is by sloppiness on the part of the administration, nothing else, because there is no other way I can explain these mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So to your knowledge this mistake was -- wasn't discovered or you certainly weren't aware of it before today, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is the first time I see it, today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as far as you know there was never any apology by Mr. Milutinovic or the government for chastising him and others for not attending meetings that they may not have actually received timely notice of, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's just one meeting, one meeting, scheduled for a particular day in November. But that would not be the right thing to conclude after all because the same treatment was received by Mr. Radenko Krulj, Professor Dr. Radenko Krulj, who was otherwise an ethnic Serb. So obviously this is a big mistake by the administration, a big mistake made, not only for the Kosovar Albanians but also for the Serbs. Radenko Krulj received the same kind of information just like Mr. Rugova, also the representative of the Gorani. As I say once again, this is a mistake, a big-time mistake, on the part of the administration. I cannot believe that this was done intentionally. It has to do with sloppiness of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you next Exhibit 1D066, I think this is at tab 36 of your binder. This is -- I believe it's a three-page exhibit. And the first page you see should be another sort of archival cover page, indicating this was sent by President Milutinovic. It's a letter to Dr. Qosja, Mr. Hyseni, and Adem Demaqi, an invitation to a meeting and it looks like it was sent on the 18th of November, 1998. Under the remarks, I see that there's handwritten text which is translated here as "Olja," O-l-j-a, or anyone else on duty give, name illegible, these letters to take by 0915 hours. Do you happen to know who Olja is?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably a person from the secretariat of the president of the republic, from the staff, from the administration of the president of the republic. Olja cannot be a name. It can only be -- well, how should I put this? A nickname, a nickname. That person certainly has to have a different real name like Olga or Olivera, but not Olja.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. If you turn to the next page, there are three identical letters addressed to Mr. Qosja, Mr. Demaqi, and Mr. Hyseni. Although the cover sheet says the 18th of November, the date on the letters themselves says the 19th of November, signed by Milan Milutinovic, and it's an invitation to a meeting suggested to take place on Friday, the 20th of November, the next date from the date on the letter in Belgrade at a time suitable to the recipient of the letter. And it does, in fairness, propose that if the reader is willing to attend, that air transport can be arranged with the assistance of Mr. Andjelkovic from the provisional Executive Council. But you will agree with me, it does seem to be a very short turnaround for a meeting proposed to take place on Friday, the 20th, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very short notice, but everyone who wants to resolve an important issue that vitally affects citizens in a particular area -- well, the shorter the notice, the greater the readiness to resolve the said issue, but, yes, it is short notice, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Related to those letters, let me show you now Exhibit 1D67. I don't think you have a tab for this one. I have a hard copy the usher can hand you, and the rest of us can follow along in e-court. I think the -- oh, I see you do have a tab. I'm sorry, it looks like it's tab 40 for you if you want to use that one instead. But the first sheet in that batch of three documents appears to be a fax from someone signed as Slana, S-l-a-n-a. Do you happen to know who that was?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't know who Slana is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And this cover document appears to be a fax forwarding an attached letter to President Milutinovic from Mr. Qosja and Mr. Hyseni, requesting that it be forwarded, noting that they had received the attached letter apparently on the 20th of November, the Friday date that the meeting we had just talked about Mr. Milutinovic sending an invitation for was scheduled. And it seems that the original letter from Mr. Hyseni and Mr. Qosja had gone to the provisional Executive Council. Now, if you would turn I think in that bundle, that three-page bundle I gave you, the second page is the original letter in Albanian with signatures. And then the third page, I believe, is the translation into Serbian for you. And I'm reading from the English translation: "Dear Mr. Milutinovic, we would like to thank you for your invitation to the discussion to find a solution to the problem in Kosovo. We continue to be engaged in finding a political solution ..." I'm skipping a bit: "However, we do not believe that improvised and hasty private discussions can contribute to such a goal. Naturally, we cannot attend any such discussions. A lasting and fair solution to the question of Kosovo implies the need for a well-prepared process of discussions among equals, unconditioned, without any imposed framework, without prejudice, and with the direct engagement of authorised international factors." Signed by Mr. Qosja and Mr. Hyseni. Were you aware that there had been a response to that invitation?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But having read that now and bearing in mind the circumstances in which the invitation apparently was sent on the 19th for a meeting on the 20th, in fairness would you agree that some of the complaint here seemed to be legitimate, that they don't want to participate in what they refer to as a "improvised and hasty" private discussion. That's fair, isn't it? Talking about this particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the way it can be understood, too, but it can also be understood to mean an agreement on the beginning of the talks. This first meeting, people would not move on straight away to establishing a final agreement or a final document. It can also be a discussion as to how future work would be carried out on premises for future work. It can be understood that way as well; it can also be understood this way as well, as Mr. Qosja understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let's move on to Exhibit 1D91, this is tab 42 in your binder, Professor. And I think this is the document -- I believe this is a document that you referred to as the Pristina Agreement.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as I recall when you testified, we found out that that copy of the document does not contain the signatures, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this copy that is provided here, no, there are no signatures contained. But signatures were placed, though. The Politika daily published this with the signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, and I think that's Exhibit 1D671 that we talked about. My question had to do with the parties signing. None of the representatives of the largest Kosovar Albanian political parties were involved in signing that document, correct, not Dr. Rugova, not Mr. Agani or Adem Demaqi or any of those?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, only Mr. Faik Jashari, Mr. Sokol Qosja they're the only ones who signed it on behalf of their small Albanian political parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And the others who signed were members of the Gorani community, the Egyptian community, and the other smaller minority groups in Kosovo, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Turks, Roma.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, let me move now to the 9th of August, last Thursday. And I want to look at I think it is Exhibit 1D443, which I believe is tab 50 in your binder. If I can find the reference in the transcript at page 13185 was when you were asked about this. And you noted that in part 5, item 2, the National Assembly of Serbia formulated principles based on which the crisis in Kosovo can be resolved. I think it's the third item from the bottom which says that Kosovo-Metohija cannot be granted the status of a republic but: "Autonomy within Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia according to the highest international standards." What were the highest international standards? You're referring to the highest international standards for autonomy in that context?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is precisely what I'm referring to and not to minority rights. Autonomy, according to the highest international standards. Although, as I said the last time around, there are no international standards for autonomy. There are perhaps comparative legal standards, but the issue of autonomy is a domestic issue for any sovereign state, and that is why no international standards can be established. One can have comparative legal standards, though. There are about 15 countries in the world that have territorial autonomy. Based on their experience, one can establish certain comparative legal standards, but no binding ones, not ones that could be binding for any country. The international community cannot foist a thing like that on any country, cannot force any country to have any form of internal autonomy at any level. This is a domestic matter and it's also a matter of the country's constitutional sovereignty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've given a statement here that there are about 15 countries in the world that have territorial autonomy. Can you give us an example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Italy, Spain, Great Britain, Portugal, Denmark. The most typical autonomy, formal autonomy, is that found in Italy and Spain since throughout the territory of these two countries there is a whole network of autonomous units. As for these other countries that I've mentioned, there are certain portions of their territories enjoying a degree of autonomy, but those countries are not -- do not comprise whole networks of autonomal [sic] units such as the case as Italy and Spain. And then further examples, those of Finland and so on and so forth. Some of the countries occurring to me right now that have territorial autonomy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is Germany not such a country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Germany is a federation; it has federal units. As a federation, it set the example for a great number of other European federations, it was used as a model. When the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was adopted in 1990, it adopted some of the solutions found in the 1949 German Grundgesetz, Basic Law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, based on doing some sort of comparative analysis of the standards of autonomy in those 15 or so countries where something like that exist, what was -- can you give us an example of what the highest standard would include for an autonomous entity?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meaning of "autonomy" is this: The population of an autonomous unit makes its own laws, adopts its own laws through bodies that it elects. These are used to define their peculiarities and typical traits. To what extent can an autonomous unit pass its own laws? Well, this is something that is normally defined within the constitution of a country. The two words "autos" and "nomos" what that means in ancient Greek is that you pass your own laws whenever your peculiarities require special laws. Any autonomy has executive bodies. It does not have the power to adopt a constitution, nor is its judiciary independent from the judiciary of the federal state. These would be a handful of European standards for autonomy which are generally applied throughout the world. If you have a unit enjoying territorial autonomy, this doesn't mean that it can ever become a state within a state; not even a federal unit can be a state within a state. Federal bodies always retain their supremacy and all of the laws of this autonomous unit must be consistent with the laws of the federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I guess if -- Professor, if I were a lawyer advocating on behalf of Kosovo in a discussion about this and saying to the National Assembly that you say I can't have the status of a republic but I can have autonomy according to the highest international standards, I would argue to you: Fine, just give me those or that degree of autonomy that we had in Kosovo between 1974 and 1989. Wouldn't you agree that that was a highest international standard for autonomy? Nobody had it better than Kosovo and Vojvodina between 1974 and 1989, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. But this was an example of constitutional excess. It was demonstrated that this sort of status ultimately led to isolation and to a desire on the part of the unit to secede from the federal country to which it belongs. This is the imperfection of the system, the imperfection of that particular model. That type of autonomy breeds a desire to have more and for this autonomy to grow and evolve into independence. This, at the time, applied to both Vojvodina and Kosovo and Metohija. This is a considerable inherent danger. That is why probably there is no country in the world endowing any of its autonomous unit with such powers, and you are entirely right in what you say about the 1974 constitution. This was an unrealistic constitution, and the best proof we need of this is the end that the country eventually met. The country eventually fell apart. The constitution set no boundaries in terms of decentralisation, and this is the fate that the country eventually met. We all know what it was. The country no longer exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, Professor. Let me move on to one other topic before we take our break. I want to talk to you about Rambouillet. Exhibit P967, I think it's tab 51 in your binder, is the Official Gazette noting the decision to appoint a delegation for talks in France. You're appointed the head of the delegation and then there are 12 other named members in the gazette. My English notes that the number one delegate listed after you is Professor Vladan, the English says Kuglesic, but I think it's Kutlesic, correct, spelled K-u-t-l-e-s-i ...

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And tell us again, who did he work for? He was a part of the federal government?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, Mr. Vladan Kutlesic was federal deputy prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And we know who Mr. Sainovic was. Number 3 is Professor Vladimir Stambuk. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a university professor. He teaches at the Faculty of Political Sciences. At the time he was holding a public post. He was the deputy chairman of the National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And he was a Serb?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not an ethnic Serb, not as far as I know. I think he spoke of himself as a Yugoslav. That was his commitment, but it's always difficult to comment on another person's ethnic commitments. Perhaps you should ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I know when you mentioned this delegation before you said of the 13 members only four were Serbs. So I take it that would include you, Mr. Sainovic, Professor Kutlesic, and who would the fourth one be? Is that Mr. Zivkovic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right, the late Vojislav Zivkovic. He was the fourth Serb in this delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was he? What was his job?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an official in one of the provinces, but believe me I can't remember exactly which post he was holding back in 1999. He is an ethnic Serb living in the autonomous province. He was one of the leaders of the socialist party of Serbia, but I can't quite remember what the post that he was holding at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we take it it was a post in Kosovo and not in Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes, in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's where he had his domicile.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then number 5, Guljbehar Sabovic, member of the provincial executive -- or provisional Executive Council. Do you know his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a lady, it's a she.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my apologies to her.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Sabovic was a representative of the Turkish ethnic community.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I think for the others we can tell based on the descriptions of what community they represent or what party. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, would this be a good time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Time for a break, Professor. Please again go with the usher, and we shall resume at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [The witness takes the stand].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, I'll do my best to try and finish before the next break. We were just talking about the Rambouillet delegation and we went through the list in the gazette. Can you tell me a little bit about how your delegation went about doing its work. When it came to make decisions, did each of the 13 members have an equal vote?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need to formalise the delegation's work in that way. The delegation worked as a united team. There was harmony amongst the members of the delegation. The decisions were made by consensus, and previously each question would be discussed in depth. So there was no need to count votes. No one ever was against something that the delegation had declared as its position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I guess that moves me forward to a point I was going to address later. Are you familiar with Professor Weller's book about the Rambouillet negotiations?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't read the book. I did read a lot of books about Rambouillet, but I didn't read that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: A number of documents from his book have been introduced by Defence counsel in this case. Let me read you a short paragraph from there and ask you for a comment. This is from 1D018 and this is the very bottom of page 401 and the top of 402. "Both parties also issued general statements of their positions in the first days of the conference. The negotiators then reported to the outside world that the delegations had requested computers and had set to work in a business-like way. While computers and other conference equipment had certainly been requested, it was in fact only Kosovo which gave evidence of constructive activity by devising detailed and substantive comments on the drafts which had been put forward by the Contact Group. The Yugoslav Serb delegation simply fell silent. Its members became known as the tea club, as they were seen lounging about the public areas of the chateau, enjoying refreshments throughout the day. At one stage an informal protest was made against the singing of Serb patriotic songs deep into the night in the Yugoslav Serb delegation room which disrupted the sleep of the sizeable delegations from the Contact Group, the OSCE, the EU, and others who were accommodated in the chateau." That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, we were at the castle, at the chateau from the 6th until the 23rd of February and we couldn't leave. And in that time interval, someone had a birthday or some celebration. This is just life. People were celebrating somebody's birthday at the time. From the 6th until the 23rd, there are many days in that period, you will admit, and some things like that had to happen. As far as I know, when there was such a reason that some members of the delegation would then stay back a bit later and there was a jovial tone when something like that was being celebrated. Perhaps somebody did sing, but it was not something that happened very often. This is something that is made much of and it's turned into a caricature almost but far from it that things like that happened every day. Simply during those 17 days someone had a birthday and we celebrated a birthday in one of those rooms because it was not possible to go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to the named delegates in the gazette, there was some other non-official, I guess, members of the contingent, correct? Wasn't Dragan Hadzi Antic, an editor of the Politika, present?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was present only from time to time. He wasn't a member of the delegation. He didn't come with the delegation. For the most part, he was there when President Milutinovic had press conferences.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Ambassador Petritsch told us that there were also a couple of additional persons listed as secretaries. Do you know who that referred to?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that there were two experts, experts in international law. The late Dr. Miodrag Mitic and Professor Etinski. Then there were two high-ranking officials of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs and a number of aides who were there to assist with computer work, copying, and distribution of the materials. That was the team that came from Belgrade to Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you mentioned at page 13194 that Mr. Milutinovic then also came to Rambouillet, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At one point of the Rambouillet negotiations, President Milutinovic arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know whose idea it was for him to attend? Was that Mr. Milosevic's idea? Mr. Milutinovic's? Or yours, as head of the delegation? Who decided that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Milutinovic himself had the idea. He was the president of the Republic of Serbia, the head of the Serbian state, and the whole situation was happening at a part of the territory of the Republic of Serbia. So it was quite natural for him, regardless of there being an official state delegation for him as the head of the state to be interested in the course of the talks, particularly because the delegation was denied freedom of movement. Let me put it that way. We were confined to the chateau premises. We couldn't leave the chateau and we couldn't have contacts with the political officials outside of the Rambouillet chateau.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But the accommodations there weren't too uncomfortable, were they?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, if I were to say that I was the only one to have a bathroom attached to the room and no one else, then you can see for yourself whether the accommodation was good. I was the head of the delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did Mr. Milutinovic have a bathroom when he came?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Milutinovic did not stay at the chateau in Rambouillet. He was staying in Paris. He would just come, conduct the talks at the chateau, and then he would return to Paris where he was staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How come he wasn't under chateau arrest like the rest of you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he was not formally a member of the delegation. Only the delegations were confined to the chateau in Rambouillet. He was the head of state.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic was a part of the official delegation. Wasn't he permitted to leave at one time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but a special permit or a special permission had to be sought. You could not leave of your own accord without the agreement of the internal protocol, let's say, in the chateau. The officer who was assigned to that duty, probably an officer from the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And he was allowed to leave and go back to Belgrade so he could consult with Mr. Milosevic about the negotiations, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I recall, he left once. He went to Belgrade once from the chateau.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That wasn't my question, though, Professor. The purpose for his leaving was to go back to Belgrade and consult with Mr. Milosevic, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say right now whether that was just with Mr. Milosevic, but in any case to consult perhaps with officials of the Republic of Serbia, with the prime minister of the Republic of Serbia, the president of the Assembly and so on. I don't know who were the people that he talked with when he was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Come now, Professor, you were the head of the delegation. You don't know who he went to talk with either before he left or after he came back, you didn't get any information about who he consulted with?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Fila on his feet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection, Your Honours. He was asked once, he was asked twice, and he said that he didn't know who the people were that he consulted with. How many more times does he have to answer and how many times does he have to be asked in order to reply to Mr. Hannis's satisfaction? He was asked and he did answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The first time the witness did not answer the question. The second time he did answer the question, and now Mr. Hannis is putting a particular point to him about his role as the leader of the delegation and the activity of a member of the delegation who went back to Belgrade and came back again. In other words, he's challenging the answer. He's wanting to take it a step further. This is not a situation of repetition, and therefore we repel the objection. He will be allowed to ask the question and have it answered. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, do you recall my question or should I repeat it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall it, but I need to warn you right away. The relationships were not hierarchical. I as the head of the delegation did not have any powers in relation to the delegation members. Each member of the delegation was an autonomous figure. Of course, Mr. Sainovic spoke with President Milosevic, but he was not obliged to report back to me and I had no right to ask him to do that. I wasn't in any position of power within the delegation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
