utterances.text: So that's not quite a straightforward answer, Professor. Are you saying you did not know why Mr. Sainovic left and you did not find out when he came back whether he had consulted with anyone? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying this, and that is the full truth: I did not ask Mr. Sainovic about the people that he talked with in Belgrade and I don't know who were all the persons that he had talked with in Belgrade. Of course he spoke with Mr. Milosevic, but I don't know if he only talked to him or -- Mr. Sainovic was the deputy prime minister of the federal government. I was the deputy prime minister of the republican government. Now, to question the deputy prime minister of the federal government, for me, would be something quite inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, the Official Gazette lists you as the head of the delegation. Mr. Sainovic's name is number three on the list. I understand the point that he's a deputy prime minister of the Federation and you're one level lower in an equivalent position in the republic. But in the context of these talks in Rambouillet, you are the formal head of the delegation. And I also understand that the protocol or the rules were that none of you members of the delegation were allowed to leave the premises during the course of these talks. Now, you told us that there was an exception made and Mr. Sainovic was allowed to leave. How did that take place? Who did he have to get permission from, first of all?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He got permission from those who were in charge on behalf of the French state of security at the chateau. I don't know who the specific person was. Believe me, I had a lot to do in relation to the annexes to the Rambouillet agreement, and I worked on the texts of these agreements very intensively. And I was busy with these questions late into the night, so I didn't really bother with such details.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, as deputy prime minister of Yugoslavia and one of the four Serbs on your delegation, he was a fairly important member of your delegation, was he not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of the delegation, just like the other 12 members of the delegation, but he was also the deputy prime minister of the federal government. Mr. Sainovic is a person of considerable political experience, too, able to communicate with people. He's an engineer by profession, so it was quite normal that there was a division of labour amongst the members of the delegation. Mr. Kutlesic and myself mostly dealt with the text of the draft agreement in Rambouillet and we worked exclusively with Mr. O'Brien and Mr. Etinski. So it was normal that Mr. Sainovic, who is not a lawyer by profession, would not be so intensively busy with the phrasing and the formulations in the draft text.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But on the issue of knowing about whether a member of your delegation was going to be present or absent and where he was going and when he was going, I suggest, Professor, that the evidence indicates that you would be in a position to know. We saw several documents where you're communicating with the co-chairman of the talks, I think where you're asking to have face-to-face meeting with the Albanian delegation, when you're asking about this document and that other document, when you're requesting if a meeting can be held at 2.00 in the afternoon. I saw some days where there were at least three or four written communications from you to the chairperson of the delegation. Are you telling us you weren't aware that Mr. Sainovic was going to go back before he left? You're not saying that, are you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't say that at any time. I did know, but there was no need for Mr. Sainovic to report back to me about the people that he talked with in Belgrade. Some open questions cropped up regarding the draft agreement text, but since he was not actually working on the text in the sense that he was formulating the text, he was not a lawyer, he was free. So he went to Belgrade to talk about those things with the people in authority in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when he returned, did he not inform you about his talk with Mr. Milosevic and what Mr. Milosevic's views were about the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did talk, but it wasn't a formal report. It wasn't a formal report what could be the position of President Milosevic when we were sent by the National Assembly and the conclusions of the National Assembly were a kind of imperative mandate for members of the Assembly. So he could think the same as the National Assembly that had sent us with those conclusions to the Rambouillet negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you about your evidence at page 13197. And you were indicating that: "We had no idea about the substance, we had no idea about the general framework of what the agreement would comprise. We had the part of the agreement that concerned the ombudsman, but we didn't have the essential parts of the agreement even as late as the 13th of February." Technically I understand that, but Ambassador Petritsch told us that as long ago as September of 1998 there was a first draft of what later turned out to be a working document in Rambouillet, there was a first document presented by Christopher Hill to Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Milosevic and some of their experts. And as early as October of 1998, Christopher Hill already had a third or a fourth version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I don't see how this can be correct. I mean I don't know wherefrom my learned colleague is gathering this. That the first -- that the first draft was shown in September 1998 to Mr. Milosevic and Milutinovic. I don't believe we had evidence like that. This is just pure fabrication in a sense and that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm referring to page 10711 of our transcript where I understand Ambassador Petritsch talks about this, and I'm talking about the substance of the proposed agreements. I'm suggesting that the broad outlines of these were known well before February 13th. It wasn't like this was a total surprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the date of that transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't have the date, Your Honour, I just have the page number. Oh, it looks like 28 February 2007, page 10711 beginning at line 4 and at line 17 Mr. Petritsch says: "So by the time we met in Rambouillet, both sides already knew the political, the civilian aspects of a possible deal pretty well."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, do you still object to this question, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, this part as I understand it on 10711 talks about the Hill process. It doesn't refer to Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it goes on to say: "It was about the fourth, fifth, or even sixth version that then became the basis, so to speak, of the Rambouillet accords. So by the time we met in Rambouillet, they already knew the political, the civilian aspects of a possible" -- and I can't read the last word there --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: "Deal" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: "Deal."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- "pretty well."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We withdraw the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue with the question, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, isn't it, Professor, that what eventually came to be the underlying basis, the rough outlines of the proposed Rambouillet agreements was something that had been talked about for months; and you were aware of that, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. First of all, it's not correct that I said that we just had the section on the ombudsman, and I don't know if that's what the transcript said. I said explicitly that we received three chapters on the 7th, the framework agreement; we received the constitution, annex 1; and we received annex 3, elections; and we received annex 6 on the ombudsman. That's one thing. Second, you said yourself or Mr. Petritsch himself said that the civilian part of the agreement was known in general but not the entire agreement. And I told you myself that we had several versions of local governance that we laid down with Mr. Hill. We talked about it, and I said when I read the text of the constitution that I recognised many places from the things offered by Mr. Hill in that plan and from the text of the annex on the constitution from the Rambouillet agreement. And Mr. Petritsch is right, that many provisions of the civilian section were known. We also called it the political part of the Rambouillet agreement as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Professor, my question was based on what I read in your testimony on the 9th of August, page 13197, line 18 and you said: "No, we had no idea about the substance, we had no idea about the general framework of what the agreement would comprise," and perhaps it's a matter of language and translation and interpretation, but I took "general framework," and the constitution would be part of the general framework, for the proposed agreement, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The constitution is one of the annexes or as they were later termed chapters of the agreement. It is chapter 1, in fact. The framework agreement precedes the constitution. The Rambouillet accords comprise the constitution chapter and eight annexes, chapters, that are separate. The first chapter or annex, as it was called previously, is the Constitution for Kosovo. And, as I said, as early as the morning of the 7th we received a framework agreement on the constitution, the elections, and the ombudsman and not just the section on the ombudsman. I do remember that very clearly. I do remember providing that particular answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Regarding the annexes, at page 13201 you mentioned annex number 8 and you said: "It was an artificial product." First of all, tell us, what was annex 8, what did that refer to?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Annex 8 was about the agreement or amendments to the agreement. It envisaged a procedure for amending the agreement. It was said there that the agreement was provisional, that it can only be amended based on an agreement between the signatories, and it was also said that three years later, there would be an international conference to deal with the Kosovo issue once and for all. That was the substance. This was the briefest of all the chapters. When the Rambouillet accords had been handed to us in parts, in separate portions, this was a separate part of the agreement; then later it was phrased as an annex, as a separate chapter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The framework agreement, that's what I think it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, in some ways that sounds analogous to the constitutional law on implementing the constitution. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a mixture between the constitutional provisions on amending the constitution and the law on implementing the amendments in a minimalistic way with precious little words and precious little articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Professor, I understand your complaint about being handed these documents on -- at the 11th hour, in effect, I think that's a legitimate complaint about late delivery. But for one thing, earlier you had written a letter to the chairman regarding certain documents that had been presented to you that you considered those to be non-existent because they hadn't been previously adopted by the Contact Group. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is about chapters 2, 5, and 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And on the other hand, one of your complaints during the course of Rambouillet was not being able to meet face-to-face with the Albanians, with their delegation, which seems to suggest that you wanted to try and work out things without internationals, just one on one, your delegation and the Albanians, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there wasn't meant to be any exclusion of the international players. No one tried to rule out their presence, but we simply gave preference or priority, if you like, to direct talks rather than exchanging standpoints and positions through intermediaries. For example, we tell these intermediaries what our position is on a certain annex and these intermediaries go to see the Albanian delegation to tell them about our position, and they walk back over to us to tell us about the position of the Albanian delegation. So rather than use this roundabout method, we wanted to have negotiations, direct talks, in the presence of the negotiating troika, but direct talks without necessarily [as interpreted] excluding the negotiators at any point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you say "without necessarily excluding" the international negotiators, I guess I had the impression from reading your request to the chairman that you intended only to speak directly with them without the internationals. But I understand now you're telling me, No, you intended for them to be present as well. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe Professor said without ever excluding the international negotiators at any point -- the negotiators at any point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you repeat that part of your answer, please answer, Professor. You said rather than using the roundabout method, we wanted to have negotiations, direct talks in the presence of the negotiating troika, but direct talks. And then you made mention of whether or not the negotiators would be excluded. What did you say on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said it was never our request to exclude the negotiators, to rule out their presence. If we could have succeeded in having the two delegations meet directly, this would not have meant the negotiators were not there. What we did not want to have is the negotiators acting as intermediaries passing messages between the two delegations. We wanted to have the two delegations facing each other directly in their presence exchanging views. I have just repeated it. I hope that satisfies your demand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I just wanted you to repeat the words you had used. Now, Mr. Hannis, do you want to go back to the question that was interrupted or are you happy with the answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I'm satisfied at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. At page 13213, you mentioned that when you returned to Belgrade your delegation was not criticised at all for your positions or your conduct during the negotiations. And I would suggest that part of that reason is because, I mean, you had President Milutinovic there part of the time, you had Mr. Sainovic there, he had gone back and spoke to Mr. Milosevic and came back to you. It seems unlikely, sir, that you were going to do anything that would have made people back home unhappy. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that, what I had in mind was the public in the Republic of Serbia. We enjoyed public support for our position. In that sense, there was no criticism, no criticism of what we did at Rambouillet. So, first and foremost, what I had in mind was the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters can't hear counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On several occasions, Professor said that when Sainovic travelled to Belgrade and spoke to a number of different people, including the relevant officials, whereas the Prosecutor is claiming only that he was at this meeting with Milosevic. This is just not true. I have to object to the way this question is being phrased. Mr. Markovic said a number of times that he had been meeting with a number of different people including Milosevic. By the way the question is being phrased, it would seem that what is being suggested that he only went there to see Milosevic and to travel straight back. The insinuation is probably that this was a private conversation between Milosevic and him and this theory is being repeated. That is the gist of our problem. If you have to say something, please say the truth, if you can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not disputing that he may have spoken with others, I just wanted to establish the fact that Mr. Milosevic was one of the ones he spoke to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm satisfied. I'm satisfied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your observations are noted, Mr. Fila. We can proceed with the next question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 13213, you mentioned that the delegation was prepared, provided that some corrections were made in the offered text, to proceed with that. Let me find the exact page, Professor, so I can make sure I have it in context. Yes, the question Mr. Zecevic asked you at line 11 on that page was: "Tell me, was the delegation prepared to accept the political agreement from Rambouillet or part of the political agreement from Rambouillet?" And your answer was: "The document was -- the delegation was prepared, provided that some corrections were made." Do you recall now what the corrections were that you wanted made before signing?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The changes or corrections requested by our delegation were in relation to implementing the general elements and principles espoused by the Contact Group. One of those principles was this: The result of the Rambouillet talks would not be allowed to impinge on the territorial integrity of the Republic of Serbia, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, or indeed any of its neighbours. However, the Kosovo constitution which was the predominant part of the political agreement, or as Mr. Petritsch referred to it, the civilian part, the political part, these are synonymous, of course, the Kosovo constitution was conceived in such a way that there was local self-government on Kosovo for as long as the state of Serbia was not in Kosovo. In no way did the state of Serbia preserve the attributes of statehood under this Kosovo constitution, and that's what our intervention was about. We wanted the constitution to reflect the fact that Kosovo was an integral part of the Republic of Serbia, and that the Republic of Serbia had all state powers in both Kosovo and Metohija. We didn't want the constitution to reflect that Kosovo and Metohija were a state within a state. That is not encouched in explicit terms but you can see it has the executive, the judiciary, the legislation. All the more, Serbia is taking up the responsibility of amending its own constitution just in order to bring its own constitution into some sort of harmony with the Kosovo constitution which is exactly the other way around. You're making the whole fit the part instead of making the part fit the whole. That's what our objections were about. Many of the solutions offered there were quite acceptable. Those were solutions arrived at through a series of long talks with the associates of Mr. Hill. Had better attention been paid to detail and had more understanding been shown for our own native legal system, because the people facing us were Americans and their legal background is, as a rule, quite different from ours, but many of the things needed to be explained to them as though they were law students or something for them to understand what we were talking about. Had there been a little more patience I think the political side of the agreement could have been agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, at page 13221 in answer to one of Mr. Zecevic's questions, you told us that you're convinced that the Government of the Republic of Serbia sincerely wanted for the situation in Kosovo and Metohija to be resolved. And in the context of your answer, I take that to mean that you were convinced that they wanted to do it peacefully? Or did you mean by any means?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first thing always in these appeals for a solution on Kosovo and Metohija was to have a political dialogue, to do it by peaceful means, rather than by armed conflict. Any armed conflict can only produce a temporary solution. If you have a political dialogue you can have lasting and meaningful solutions, and that is what I had in mind. You can see that if you look at any of the statements and public declarations made by President Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm aware of those statements. I want to ask you, though, in Yugoslavia at that time was the issue of Kosovo going to be -- could it have been resolved without the agreement or consent of Mr. Milosevic? Isn't it a fact that that could not have been accomplished unless he was agreeable to whatever the means was?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm unable to agree with you. President Milosevic did not have the sort of power under the 1992 constitution, the sort of power that you suggest he had. He was the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and he only had the powers that he had under the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Over and above that, he would have run the risk of being in violation of the constitution and he would have run the risk of being recalled.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm asking you not only about his de jure authority, but about his de facto power. And he had tremendous power in Yugoslavia at that time, did he not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd rather say that he enjoyed an enormous reputation among the citizens at the time, and he enjoyed their endless trust. He emanated authority. As for his powers, the Constitutional Court never found him to have acted outside the boundaries defined in the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the power that he held in the 1990s and in 1999 stemmed in part from his connection with Kosovo and his position on Kosovo; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was certainly one of the reasons for the fact that all the citizens trusted him so much. But there were other personal qualities that accounted for this. I said at the very outset, President Milosevic was an exceptionally charismatic person. He had a great reputation with the majority of Yugoslavia's citizens. The elections clearly showed that when he was elected president of the republic by what you might term a landslide majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I would suggest to you, Professor, that he, Mr. Milosevic, in late 1998 and 1999 had a sincere dissolve -- sincere resolve to try and solve the problem in Kosovo; however, I would suggest to you that he was willing to solve the problem by other than peaceful means. You would agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I would. I'm entirely certain about this. President Milosevic wanted for the whole thing to be resolved by peaceful means. However, if you have someone trying to break away from a sovereign state and declare themselves to be a sovereign state, then this is the party causing the conflict and not the party trying to preserve territorial integrity. Their desire brought this about. There is not a single country in the world that would just stand by and watch as a part of its territory is trying to break away and constitute itself as another country, another sovereign country. It is this other party that had no intention of a peaceful solution for Kosovo and Metohija precisely because of what drove them on. It wasn't President Milosevic who brought this about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, you're aware of an agreement that was signed with President Milosevic and representatives from NATO, General Clark and General Naumann, on the 25th of October, 1998?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never seen the actual text.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you were aware of the existence of such an agreement, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a news item, I'd heard of it but I had no idea about the specific wording.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware of the general terms of that agreement?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said, I've never actually seen it. It's never been handed to me to read. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Professor at the time you were one of the five deputy prime ministers for Serbia. This agreement had a significant effect on what was going to happen in Kosovo with regard to withdrawing members from the MUP and making changes about the deployment of the army, the coming of the OSCE Kosovo mission. You weren't aware of that agreement or the general parameters of that agreement?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I told you that I was. I had been informed. The news reached me, but I was not familiar with the text of the agreement. What you are saying now is something that I learned based on hearsay at the time. Even what you're telling me now is second-hand information, as opposed to reading the actual text, which I never have. As for everything else you're telling me, this is all something I read about in the papers but I didn't read the actual document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, before -- I got sidetracked a little bit on that, Professor. The point I was trying to make was that I suggest to you that Mr. Milosevic was determined to solve the problem in Kosovo and he was willing to do it by means other than peaceful means. And I would ask if your opinion about that -- which you've told me is, that's not correct. I ask if your opinion would change if you knew that he had said on the 25th of October, 1998, that he would find a solution for the Kosovo problem in the spring of 1999 and he would do what was done in Drenica in 1945. I further explain to you that to General Naumann and Clark, that that meant taking them out and shooting them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we object. This calls for speculation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure I follow that objection. What's being put is something that's been said in the evidence here, and the witness is being asked if knowing this changes his opinion about the attitude of Mr. Milosevic to finding a peaceful solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I would suggest that it should be established first that the witness is aware of these words of President Milosevic, and only then ask him what would be the conclusion on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That objection is repelled. There's no reason why the witness has to have prior knowledge before today of these -- for this question to be relevantly put to him. Therefore, you may proceed with the question, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, should I repeat the question or do you have it in mind?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. But I didn't hear that. I wasn't at that meeting or lunch or whatever. This is all in the realm of speculation. You can go on telling me different things, asking for my opinion like this, but the simple truth is I don't know about these matters. I, for one, very much doubt the authenticity of what you're suggesting or the veracity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, set that aside for a moment because we do have evidence under oath from General Naumann that that was said. I'm just asking you to accept that for the purpose of this hypothetical. If you knew Mr. Milosevic had said words to those -- to that effect, would that change your opinion about whether Mr. Milosevic was resolving to use other than peaceful means to solve the Kosovo problem? Would it change your opinion or not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would if this was something that he stated for the public, if this was something that he announced over the state television, for example, to Serbia's citizens; but you're talking about a private conversation. I'm not sure what the tone of that conversation was. Something like this being said, I wouldn't take this at face value, as people say, where I come from. It would change my opinion if this was something that he actually announced to the public in his capacity as the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Now, as for any statements he may or may not have made in private meetings in his capacity as a private person, I wouldn't attach quite the same sort of weight to those possibilities. Knowing that he may have said this in a private conversation, on a private occasion at a lunch or a function or something like that, well, I am a lawyer and this certainly wouldn't constitute a good enough reason for me to change my opinion. What I find to be of importance are public statements, statements made in a public or official capacity. Private conversations are a different matter entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure I understand that distinction, Professor, but let me move on. I'll have a question for you about a public statement by someone else later on. Regarding the Rambouillet conference at the end of those first meetings, I think it's Exhibit P625, I think it's -- that's the same exhibit as P -- ID582 [sic]. I'm not sure we have a tab for that. I have a hard copy we could hand you, Professor, and this is a letter from -- I see -- I'm sorry, it is in the binder, tab 66. But this is a letter dated the 23rd of February from you to Mr. Hill, Mr. Petritsch, and Mr. Mayorski. And basically, it seems to be a fairly positive letter regarding what had happened so far in Rambouillet. You note in the first paragraph that major progress had been achieved in the talks. In the third paragraph, you note that you're ready to participate in the next meeting on the issue. In the final paragraph, that the Republic of Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia are fully ready to continue the work in line with the: "Positive spirit of this meeting." Is this an accurate -- an accurate reflection of your position about the talks as of 23rd February 1999?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not quite. But out of respect for the organisers and their efforts for the conference to succeed and the fact that the conference would be continued, it was a bit dressed up, if I can put it that way, this comment regarding the result of the talks in Rambouillet. This was mostly done out of consideration to the organisers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I guess that takes me to my next question then because as a matter of fact you and Mr. Milutinovic had a -- had a press conference later on, I think, where you were extremely critical of what had been going on in Rambouillet, is that correct, or was that only after the Paris talks?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd have to see those texts. To this day I have a critical view towards the talks in Rambouillet and in Paris at that. I presented that criticism in the report that I submitted to the National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you say your letter in Exhibit P625 or 1D582 was dressed up. I take it that's sort of polite talk for, Well, that wasn't actually the whole truth of how we felt about it, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. We pointed out a few times that there weren't any real negotiations, that the political part had to go through some additional corrections; and finally, that two documents appeared that hadn't been discussed at all beforehand by the Contact Group and they were being submitted on behalf of the Contact Group. This is chapters 2 and 7 or annexes 2 and 7 to the agreement, as you wish. So all of that was not mentioned out of consideration to the organiser. After all, this is a diplomatic, polite form of address. If one were to discuss this in greater detail --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop -- I'm going to stop you there, Professor. Is there any purpose being served by this, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to make a connection now to what you had said previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Professor, while we were talking about Mr. Milosevic's comments as reported by General Naumann, you drew a distinction between statements that might have been made in public to the Serbian people, that you would give greater weight, those public statements as opposed to the private statement that he apparently made. Yet, here you seem to be saying, Well, yeah, in my letter, in my public letter to the negotiators of the conference I wasn't really telling the truth. That seemed to be just the opposite. Can you explain that for me?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not say that we weren't telling the truth. This letter is not untruthful. However, the shortcomings were not referred to. Because the conference was supposed to continue and then are you supposed to say what the deficiencies were at Rambouillet? In a way, in this way, you are handicapping the sequel to the conference. This letter is not a detailed report. This letter is supposed to convey a message on the readiness of the delegation for the talks to continue. And if you are advocating the continuation of the talks, then it's not proper for you to refer to all the shortcomings of the talks during the first stage. That is what you're going to say in the continuation of the talks. This cannot be a detailed report on our objections to the way the discussions in Rambouillet took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me move on to page 13226. Mr. Zecevic asked you if you had ever heard President Milutinovic saying anything along the lines of: If Yugoslavia was going to be subjected to bombings or air-raids, it would lead to a massacre in Kosovo. Now, you said you never heard anything like that, but as a matter of fact, Professor, during your time in Rambouillet you weren't in Mr. Milutinovic's presence the entire time that he was there, were you? You weren't his personal body-guard.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So you cannot know for certain, can you, whether or not Mr. Milutinovic may have had a conversation with Ambassador Petritsch when you weren't present?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you yourself in the first part of your question said that I had said that I had not heard of any such thing, so that does not rule the possibility of the other party having said something like that. But I did not hear that and that is how you started your very own question. I cannot know what President Milutinovic discussed with Mr. Petritsch when I was not present at those talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to Mr. Milutinovic's activities during the war between March 24th and June when the conflict ended, did you have -- well, what level of contact did you have with him? Did you see him on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry, what was the interval? My concentration seems to be going down. What's the interval, from the 24th of - what? - February?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: 24th of March, 1999, during the NATO bombing, during those 79 days.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw President Milutinovic only a few times during that period of time, primarily in relation to those decrees that were referred to whose text was drafted by the government and he was supposed to adopt them; and I, on behalf of the government, signed the cover letter. That's the only times I saw him. On other occasions, I did not see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I think the only other significant time you had contact with him would have been then that time you went to Pristina with him on, I think, the 28th of April, 1999, to see Dr. Rugova, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes, yes. And -- well, yes, I was present there too as well -- there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how did you travel to that meeting? Did you and he travel together by plane or were you driven there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had we travelled by plane, you'd have no one to talk to now. We travelled by car. That's the only way we would have reached Pristina alive, and even that was at a great risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was it just the two of you accompanied by whoever the official driver and security personnel were? But were there any other authorities, government officials?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember, I cannot claim anything with certainty, I think it was only the persons that you referred to just now. I cannot remember whether there was anyone else there, any public office holder.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, how did you happen to go on that trip? Did you volunteer or were you requested to go? How did that come about?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know -- well, I was in the government and I figured prominently in these negotiations from 1998 and I was in Rambouillet and Paris, the head of the delegation. Mr. Rugova was also on the delegation, and it was only natural that some other office holder should accompany President Milutinovic, someone who had taken part in the previous talks with the delegation of the Kosmet Albanians. I didn't really ask to go. Probably it was President Milutinovic who had asked me to go along with him for reasons that were quite understandable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Were you aware at that time that Dr. Rugova and his family had been basically under house arrest for some weeks and that the international community was pressing the Serb leadership to release him?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that he had been under house arrest or do I believe that he had been under house arrest. It is probable that for quite understandable reasons Mr. Rugova had to have a security detail from our police. And that security provided for him as a person is not something that I could call house arrest. However, I claim -- well, I don't know anything with any certainty about any of that. I just assert that Mr. Rugova had strong security because the situation in Kosovo and Metohija at that time was one where chaos prevailed. He himself was not trusted by the extremist -- by the extremists among the Albanian population there. He had enemies among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I take it, Professor, that you have not -- you hadn't seen or read Mr. Rugova's testimony from the Milosevic trial about the circumstances under which he found himself in April 1999?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I haven't. This was not accessible to me. I don't see how it was that I could have read this. This wasn't published anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, the trial was broadcast, Professor, the transcripts are available.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Nor, I take it, that you didn't see or read the testimony of Mr. Merovci in either this trial or Mr. Milosevic's trial?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You were present when there was -- there were cameras present recording the -- at least a portion of the meeting of Mr. Milutinovic and Mr. Rugova on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing any armed soldiers or policemen in the room when that took place?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say anything for sure, but it is with a great deal of certitude that I can assume that they were there because as the president of the state of Serbia and the leader of the Kosmet Albanians. According to their constitution, he's the president of their republic, of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you -- were you aware of the nature of the relationship between Mr. Milutinovic and Mr. Milosevic at that time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a private matter. I cannot say. The two of them know that the best.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have any occasion to observe the two of them together or have any knowledge about their public working relationship?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for their public relations, they were intensive for a simple reason. It was the president of the federal republic and the president of a federal unit, the president of the Republic of Serbia that had the problem that it had. And it's only natural that the federal republic, which is an international subject; and its president, which is the organ representing the federal state; and the representative of the federal state that has the problem that it has and that is being followed by the international public and the international community, it is only natural that they have intensive contacts, and those are the only contacts that I know about. As for private contacts, I cannot testify about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If I were to tell you that Mr. Milutinovic has said that because of his previous career, which was -- well, as you know, I think he was in the foreign ministry, and his experience and his honesty, Mr. Milosevic could swallow so many things which I told to him which are -- which were not so pleasant or maybe that you can call or count as closeness." Would you agree with that, that Mr. Milutinovic seemed to have an ability to tell Mr. Milosevic things that other people might not be able to get away with?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if that is what Mr. Milutinovic says, he as an immediate protagonist is certainly telling the truth. I did not have that degree of - how should I put this? - friendship, closeness in order to be in a position to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Professor, in search of archives of the presidential archives of the Republic of Serbia, one of the documents that the OTP had is a document dated the 14th of April, 1999, purportedly from you to Mr. Milutinovic about establishing and duties of the temporary Executive Council for Kosmet, and beginning principles and elements for making the fundamental document on Kosmet autonomy. Do you recall such a document?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you mean fundamental document about the autonomy of Kosovo. I don't know what document that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's only a description I have, Professor, from an archive sort of registry. If you don't know, you don't know. Let me move on to the final three things I want to ask you about. And in fairness to you, Professor, I don't know if when you were preparing for your testimony you were advised, but I or we, the Prosecution, had filed a motion to preclude you from testifying as an expert, and part of our argument was that it was our view that you were biased, too biased to testify as an expert. One of the things I want to show you is Exhibit P980. This is a video. You saw it when you testified in the Milosevic case, and it just takes a view seconds. We'll play it and I'll ask you a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: "Serbia's parliament duly backed Milosevic's rejection of the Rambouillet terms as did the Serb public. Serbia's deputy prime minister revealed what Milosevic was planning to do next."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, do you recall seeing that when you testified previously?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, that's then-Deputy Prime Minister Vojislav Seselj, who was one of the five deputy prime ministers of Serbia, and he's saying that if NATO bombs, then no Albanians will be left in Kosovo, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we all heard that. He said that many Serbs would get killed and he said what you said just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Subsequent to that, did -- did the National Assembly or did the prime minister or did the president or did Mr. Milosevic, did anybody criticise him for that particular public statement?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't any criticism; however, it is my duty to explain why. Mr. Seselj is the leader of a political party that was a coalition partner. He made appearances in two different capacities, in the capacity of the leader of a political party who cares about votes and who is motivated primarily by winning votes in the elections; and this other capacity of deputy prime minister. The statement he is making is -- well, I think this is some gathering of the Serbian Radical Party, and he is making a statement as a party leader, as the leader of the Serbian Radical Party, not as the deputy prime minister of the Republic of Serbia. After all, political people are held responsible by the public for their political statements. The electorate body does that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But as a deputy prime minister your job is 24 hours a day, seven days a week, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not the case with me. I never took a permanent job with the government. I was not paid as deputy prime minister. I never received any money for that. I volunteered in that capacity. Throughout this period I received my salary as a professor at the Law School of Belgrade University and throughout this period, I did all my work as a lecturer, I taught, I gave lectures, I had exams, I worked with my students. So I was not permanently employed by the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, you didn't make this statement, I'm not challenging you. But how does one looking at this, know that Mr. Seselj is speaking as leader of the radical party and not as deputy prime minister? He's not wearing some special hat that says, "Radical Party," not "Deputy Prime Minister." There's no indication he made some sort of qualifying statement at the beginning that these remarks are only are my personal opinion and not those of the government.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I saw on this recording was that behind him are only persons who are officials of the Serb Radical Party. There's no one from the government there. I assume -- well, probably had I seen this for a longer period of time I would have seen the flags, too. I assume that this was only a gathering of the Serb Radical Party because behind him I see Mr. Vucic, who is an official of the Serb Radical Party, and a few other faces. If I were to see this clip again I could tell you. All of them are from the Serb Radical Party; that is to say, that this is some kind of manifestation of their political party, not a speech made by Mr. Seselj in his capacity as deputy prime minister of the Republic of Serbia. And I repeat once again, one of the five deputy prime ministers. We have enumerated all the deputy prime ministers of that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I have two more areas to go into, one exhibit, it will take me probably 10 or 15 minutes. I had hoped to be finished by now but both the Professor and I took longer a couple times than expected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll break there for lunch, Professor, and please again go with the usher. And we'll resume at 1.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.45 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're waiting for the witness to come in, I just wanted to advise the Court and co-counsel across the hall that today -- it's quite likely the last day that we'll see Ms. Moeller here in court. She's leaving us to work for another Tribunal and I wanted to thank her on the record and wish her well on her new endeavours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for advising us of that, Mr. Hannis. It will be a disappointment to us also to see her depart, but we wish her well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one thing, Your Honours. While I was preparing for re-direct, I found that on page 57, lines 13 and 14, there is a misspelled word in the transcript. It says hole as "h-o-l-e" and it should be "w-h-o-l-e" because it refers to whole and a part. That's the only thing. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, just before the break I said I have two more topics and one more exhibit. I miscalculated. I have three topics and two exhibits. The first one relates to the 23rd of March, 1999, it's Exhibit 1D585. And I don't think you have this one in your binder, but it's a transcript of Mr. Milutinovic's remarks to the Assembly on the 23rd of March, 1999, reporting about the efforts of your delegation at the talks in Rambouillet and Paris. I have -- I think I have a hard copy that contains everything I want to ask you about. I'll have the usher hand that to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is already an exhibit in the case, Mr. Hannis, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think it's an exhibit in the case. It was on the Defence 65 ter list, but it has not yet been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, it is in the binder, but the whole stenographic record of that particular session of the Assembly, let me just -- please bear with me until I find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, well if it's in the binder, then it's an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, please proceed, Mr. Hannis. It looks as though the matter -- it is an exhibit. If Mr. Zecevic finds that that's wrong, he'll draw it to our attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's 1D32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 1D32, I am advised by my colleague Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the one that's being put to the witness is 1D585. Is it also 1D32?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This may be a smaller excerpt from the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. That is -- I'm just told that this is just an excerpt of the whole document which is 1D32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 1D32 is already an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, I think you told us before you were present that day at the Assembly when Mr. Milutinovic made these remarks?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, I was submitting my report to the National Assembly in my capacity as head of the delegation. This is the debate that had to do with the report that I submitted to the National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, and I understand you spoke as well. Did you spoke before or after Mr. Milutinovic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I addressed the Assembly before President Milutinovic addressed the Assembly because the entire debate had to do with the report that I had submitted to the National Assembly. The remarks made by President Milutinovic are related to the report that I submitted to the National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to read from three or four passages and ask you to comment. The first one is the third paragraph of my excerpt that starts with the sentence: "The subject of the talks was not an agreement. It was the troops, only troops, and nothing else but troops." Do you find that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's not an accurate assessment of the documents that were discussed, is it? There's much more being talked about than just troops.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, all subjects contained in the agreement were discussed. Troops, or rather, chapter 7, especially annex B to that particular section boiled down to troops only in practical terms, and that was quite unacceptable to our delegation especially with a view to the conclusions reached by the National Assembly. These conclusions were reached by the National Assembly before the delegation went to Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, Professor. The next paragraph I have says: "That means there will be no Yugoslav Army and police in Kosovo. That means we will have a renewed verification mission in Kosovo. Walker," I assume that means William Walker, "is a child's play in comparison with that new verification mission. We would get a new Gauleiter who would govern Kosovo." Now "Gauleiter" is a reference to -- that's a German term from World War II and associated with the Nazis and their occupying armies during World War II and leading up to World War II, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the meaning of that word.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Two paragraphs down it says: "Of course they led us to Rambouillet in order to 'strangle' us, to 'strangle us in the dark.'" Is that your assessment, is that the way you felt about it at the time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said in my report, but I submitted a formal report that I read out in the Assembly and you have the text of that report in the binder here. It exists. It precedes this debate. President Milutinovic improvised. He did not read out a speech. Of course, the tone is more familiar in remarks that are off the cuff rather than in a formal report that I submitted. So I have already said that the National Assembly has 250 MPs. You have to adjust your register, your linguistic register, to the profile of all the persons present. You really have to explain to them what it was that was going on in Rambouillet, and what was going on in Rambouillet was really an incredible pressure that was brought to bear on our delegation in order for it to adopt the proposed solutions. After all, it would be sufficient if you knew that there was an explicit threat that we would be bombed if the agreement is not signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The last one I want to read to you is the first sentence in the second paragraph after that on the next page in English it says: "It is not only about Kosovo. There's a demand to destroy the entire state of Serbia in a perfidious way in three years' time. That's the essence of the whole story." Did you agree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, if an agreement envisages that NATO forces can move throughout the territory of Serbia, as through the land of their own fathers. And if Serbia's sovereignty was to be suspended only to part of its territory, what does that mean but suspending the statehood of Serbia in its territory when there are forces that are immune to any form of responsibility, as envisaged in annex B of chapter 7 of the agreement. That's it as far as a sovereign state is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, the next thing I'd like you to help me with has to do with perhaps a cultural matter or a linguistic matter. In Serbia and in the former Republic of Yugoslavia, typically how are judges addressed in court? If you're a lawyer appearing before a judge, is there a term or a name, a style of address you use in speaking to the judge?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not an attorney, but as far as I know there is nothing in particular. You simply address a judge as: Mr. Judge. There are attorneys here and they can give a more authentic answer than I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I know that our B/C/S-speaking lawyers in this case typically use the term "casni sude," I don't know if I'm pronouncing that correctly, but that gets translated as "Your Honour" or "Your Honours," correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I saw here in The Hague for the very first time. I think that there is no such rule in our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you were a judge of the Constitutional Court, did lawyers appear before you live or is that something that's only done through written submissions without lawyers standing up in front of you and talking?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were no attorneys in that court. There were representatives of the -- the authority that passed the law that is being challenged before that court. There was no particular form of address for these judges, although the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia had the position of the highest court in the land. The only form of address was: Mr. Judge, nothing more than that. There was no special title bestowed upon a judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you say: "Mr. Judge," are you substituting "judge" for the particular name of the judge or would you say: Mr. Judge Bonomy?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll take my own example. When I was the judge rapporteur the participants in the debate would say: Judge Markovic. Judge Markovic believes, Judge Markovic said this or that. So what is stated is the office that is held and the last name of the person holding that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And would I be wrong in assuming that in your classroom you typically get - and you probably expect - your students to refer to you as: Professor Markovic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, except that students address everyone as "Professor," even those who are assistant professors and those who are lecturers. So students tend to assign that to everyone taking part in the teaching process, regardless of the actual status attained.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The reason I was inquiring about this, Professor, is that when you testified in the Milosevic trial, I reviewed the transcript and the only place -- the few places I could see where you actually addressed the Judge, you called him Mr. Robinson, I think maybe Mr. Bonomy one time. And I know Mr. Milosevic insisted on addressing the Judges as "Mr." Now, when you were prepared to testify in that case did Mr. Milosevic suggest to you that you should only call the Judges "Mr." rather than "Your Honour"?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no mention was made of that. I noticed this matter that you referred to just now and before this trial began, I asked Mr. Zecevic who is counsel here whether I should address the Court as "Your Honours" and when I should do that because I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, I noticed that the first time you addressed Judge Bonomy here you did said "Your Honour," and that was a surprise to me having read your transcript in Milosevic. All right. Professor, I wanted to move on to the last thing I had to ask you about this is Exhibit P2894. I only have this in English, Professor. Let me tell you what it is and then I'll ask you a few questions about it. This is purported to be an interview with you conducted on the 7th of July, 1999, and it appears on a web site called "Jurist: The law professors' network" and the interview is reported to have been conducted by one Professor Bernard J. Hibbitts, H-i-b-b-i-t-t-s, an associate dean at the University of Pittsburgh law school in Pennsylvania in the USA. Do you recall having participated in an e-mail interview with the "Jurist" or Professor Hibbitts?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall. A colleague of ours acted as a go-between who was a visiting professor in Pittsburgh at the time. This is a colleague who was a professor of constitutional law. After my return from Rambouillet, quite simply, he wanted me to speak for this periodical or paper, whatever it is, "Jurist." He wanted to interview me, he put a few questions to me, and after all this is a colleague, this is another professor of constitutional law, and I bore that in mind and I gave him my answers. This was also in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Was this interview conducted in English or was somebody translating for you? How did that take place? Did he send you an e-mail question and you wrote back? How did that work?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this was translated from Serbian into English. He put questions to me and I answered in Serbian and that was subsequently translated into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever have a chance to review it to be sure that what he put out was correct and accurate?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, believe it or not. I believed that it would be done properly and I think it was. When I read it, it seemed to me that the language was right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you tell us -- you do understand some English and read some English?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you tell us the name of the colleague who actually did the translating?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do not know who it was who did the translating, but it was Professor Sima Avramovic who was the go-between. He gave me the questions and then -- as for who translated this, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Then, Professor, what I'd like to do is just go to a couple -- two or three particular passages and read them to you and ask then if they're a correct statement of your views. The first one is on the second page, and I've highlighted, I think, in the copy I gave you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for Defence counsel, it's the middle of the page with the Jurist asking the question: "What actions will the Serbian government take to ensure that Serbs who have committed atrocities against members of the ethnic Albanian community in Kosovo are tried by the appropriate national and/or international Tribunals?"

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then, Professor, I'm reading from part of your answer, the third line says: " ... When Albanian extremists started their violent secession and tried to overthrow the constitutional government in Serbia, those disagreements reached a climax. There are laws and courts in Yugoslavia to handle this." Skipping one sentence. "Everyone who is responsible for criminal acts will be prosecuted for them before domestic courts and other proper state bodies." Let me pause there. What would be the other proper state bodies besides domestic courts? Would that be the military courts or were you referring to something else?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all organs, the public prosecutor if prosecution is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The next line: "The question is: Why should an international court be in charge of such acts?" Then going four lines down: "The war on Kosovo was started by NATO on March 24th, 1999, and an international court can only have the jurisdiction over crimes that NATO committed against Yugoslavia ..." Is that a correct version of your answer on that day?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that's still your opinion, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I still think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could go to the next page, and I think it's highlighted on your version, Professor. And for my learned friends, it's the -- under Deputy Prime Minister Markovic, it's the second paragraph that begins: "The indictment of President Milosevic by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia in The Hague is a transparent political game and a mocking of the court and the law. First and foremost, the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia does not enjoy a high reputation as a court." That was your opinion then. Is that still your opinion today?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, in my country there is freedom of thought and public expression of one's views. I as a citizen enjoy that freedom and I have the right to think and to express my thoughts freely. I don't know what it is that you're holding against me. My thoughts? In that case, you are attacking my constitutional freedom. I have the right to think, especially as regards matters that are within the domain of my own profession. I don't see what is so unusual here; this is quite simply my opinion, what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, please don't misunderstand me. That's all I'm trying to do is confirm that that's your opinion. In my country, we have a saying about: I may disagree with you what you say, but I'll defend to the death your right to say it. And, Professor, all I want to know is if that's what you said and if that's your opinion. So, is it your opinion today still that this court does not enjoy a high reputation as a court?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the opinion of the majority of the citizens of my country, and I'm expressing that opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that's your personal opinion, too, and that's still your opinion today, as it was in 1999, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether it is my duty to answer Mr. Hannis as to what it is that I think, and what does this have to do with this case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just give us a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, what is the purpose of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in evaluating the credibility of this witness, whether or not he has a bias towards this court is a factor that you may want to consider in deciding those questions on other matters that he's answered. Related, Your Honour, to the answers he gave about Mr. Milosevic's comments and how he might give them more or less credibility depending on whether he spoke in a private group or in front of the people of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hannis, we disagree. We do not consider it appropriate to invite the witness to express his personal opinion of the court. We do not think it's relevant to any issue in the trial. So we sustain -- well, we say to the witness that he is not obliged to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, is he obliged to answer the question about whether or not he made that statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Whether or not he made that statement in 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You already --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He's agreed he gave this interview --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- and he believes it's correct. I'm just asking about particular provisions to be sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what he said in 1999 at that stage is no more relevant than what he might be asked to say today, so there is no other question on this that we are prepared to admit, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. I will abide by your ruling. I take exception. I think it is a factor that you should consider in determining the credibility of this witness. If he has a bias to this court, to this institution, that can affect his credibility --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Move on to your next question, Mr. Hannis. We've ruled on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, learned Professor, I would like to ask you a question which will be an opinion coming from your side and I'll take it as a very learned opinion. You know as we talk of cause and effect. Now, what is your view about the leadership failures in case of reconciliation vis a vis Yugoslavia and the various ethnic nationalities, what can be the failures? Because a person like yourself dedicated to constitution and constitutionalism would always be diagnosing these things, and that will help us in appreciating what really could be the causes. I would request you to be as brief as possible, and I'm grateful that you have heard this question. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to know how to respond, are you interested in the break-up of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or just the situation in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I mean, I'd -- with all respect to my very learned colleagues, I think I'll be interested in knowing the recent happenings, not what may have happened in the past, we can read all that, what could be the failures? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The failure was the understanding about the right of a nation to self-determination as a part of a family of nations within a state. Does the right to self-determination include the right to secession? Nobody challenged that. The Constitutional Court didn't do it either, but there was a difference between the right of a nation to self-determination and a republic as a federal unit. In order to exercise the right to self-determination, it was necessary for the nationalities, the ethnic groups, to reach agreement and then to establish the mode of its implementation and not for the republics, as such, to leave the Federation. But previously they needed to reach an inter-ethnic arrangement. In this way with the secession of republics, there was a violation of the rights to the self-determination of the Yugoslav people who were a national minority within a republic. So this absence of an inter-ethnic agreement to implement the right of an ethnic group to self-determination was the cause of the war, of the conflict that was waged on the territory of the former Yugoslavia. Where is the failure? All failed because they didn't understand that and because they did not take the peaceful road and the legal road to realise their right to self-determination but chose to do it through violence and through war. In any event, in the case of President Milosevic, I interpreted the decision of the Canadian Supreme Court of 1998 about the implementation of a nation's right to self-determination, and I absolutely agree with the arguments given by the Canadian Supreme Court about why unilateral secession of a federal unit is impermissible from the point of view of the federation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And that includes what I said in this regard, the leadership failure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely, absolutely. I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. I have some matters to clear up before we proceed further. There was reference in cross-examination to three exhibits 1D551, 1D552, and 1D553, which I do not think were exhibited earlier but obviously you are the source. I take it there is no objection to the use that was made of these and that these should be regarded as exhibits in the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just bear with us, Your Honour, just one minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 1D551 is a statement of the MUP of the 5th of March, 1998, which mentioned the killing -- in fact, they are a series of documents and it's -- follows on the Jashari incident and the third one is the one where there's reference -- the first reference to civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hannis, in dealing with an exhibit P1857 referred to it as having been used by you in your examination-in-chief, but as it turns out it was not used in examination-in-chief. This is the Law on Determination of the Work of the Assembly of Kosovo, and he proceeded to ask questions about it, to which there was no objection and it's difficult to see that there could be any objection. I take it the exhibition of that document causes you no trouble?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, you had undertaken to try to clarify the situation about the web site and the IC133, which was the Serb document which appeared in three paragraphs and therefore, clarified the English translation, and indeed the Serb version of the original. Have you been able to deal with that satisfactorily?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe I have informed the Trial Chamber that we have done all that we can; namely, we have submitted our request to the judicial committee of the -- judiciary committee of the National Assembly for the -- for the proper information on the contents of that particular article of the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that one then remains --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that will be -- and I explained to the Judges that due to the vacation time they will be only end of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That remains marked for identification until you have clarified the position and made an appropriate filing. 1D18 was a reference to comments in the Weller book rather than extracts of events or meetings or legislation or texts of agreements. Has the whole of that book been exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. As a matter of fact, it has been -- only the pages which have been exhibited, the one out of 1D18, pages of the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the part which Mr. Hannis referred to, which was the description of the behaviour of the Serb delegation is --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
